lead: In an ideal solution each component's partial pressure is its liquid mole fraction times its own vapour pressure: y<sub>i</sub>P = x<sub>i</sub>P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>. That is Raoult's law. Most real pairs, such as ethanol–water, disobey it, so one correction per component is added, the activity coefficient γ<sub>i</sub>. The modified form y<sub>i</sub>P = x<sub>i</sub>γ<sub>i</sub>P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> is the working equation behind distillation and flash-drum design.
prereq: You need the equal-fugacity criterion from criteria for phase equilibrium and stability, the P-x-y diagram from phase equilibria of pure components and mixtures, and the activity coefficient with the Margules, van Laar and Wilson models.

blocks.text: At equilibrium every component has the same fugacity in the vapour and in the liquid, fiV = fiL (see 6.1). Writing each side in terms of composition gives the general starting equation.
y<sub>i</sub> φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> P = x<sub>i</sub> γ<sub>i</sub> f<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup>,pure(T, P)
blocks.where: φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> is the vapour fugacity coefficient, γ<sub>i</sub> the liquid activity coefficient, and f<sub>i</sub><sup>L,pure</sup> the fugacity of pure liquid i at the mixture T and P; P is in kPa.

blocks.text: Three assumptions reduce this to Raoult's law.

items: Ideal-gas vapour: φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> = 1. Acceptable up to a few bar.
Standard state is pure liquid i at the same T and P, with the Poynting correction neglected, so f<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup>,pure ≈ P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>, the vapour pressure of pure i at T.
Ideal solution: γ<sub>i</sub> = 1, meaning unlike molecules attract each other exactly as strongly as like molecules.

blocks.where: P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> is the vapour pressure of pure i at the system T, in kPa; Σy<sub>i</sub> = Σx<sub>i</sub> = 1.

blocks.text: For a pure component x = y = 1, and the equation collapses to P = P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>, the vapour-pressure curve. Get P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> from an Antoine correlation, ln P = A − B/(T + C), used exactly as tabulated: put T in the table's unit (K or °C), read P in its unit (kPa or mmHg), check ln against log₁₀, and convert to kPa (1 mmHg = 0.13332 kPa) before adding terms. Benzene–toluene obeys the law closely because the two molecules are similar in size and shape.

sections.h3: Modified Raoult's law and the bubble-pressure recipe

blocks.text: Drop only the third assumption. Keep the vapour ideal and keep the pure-liquid standard state. All liquid non-ideality now sits inside γ<sub>i</sub>, and γ<sub>i</sub> depends on the whole composition, not on x<sub>i</sub> alone.

blocks.where: γ<sub>i</sub> is the liquid activity coefficient at the system T and x, with γ<sub>i</sub> → 1 as x<sub>i</sub> → 1.

items: Fix T and the liquid composition x.
Get every P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> from Antoine at that T.
Evaluate every γ<sub>i</sub> at x from the chosen model (Margules, van Laar or Wilson).

blocks.text: Bubble temperature: P and x are known, but every P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> moves with T, so guess T, compute Σx<sub>i</sub>γ<sub>i</sub>P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>, and correct T until the sum equals P (second example). Dew point: y and P (or T) are known, x is not. Start with γ<sub>i</sub> = 1, compute x<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>P/(γ<sub>i</sub>P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>), normalise, recompute γ<sub>i</sub>, and repeat until Σy<sub>i</sub>/(γ<sub>i</sub>P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>) = 1/P.

blocks.where: K<sub>i</sub> is the vapour-liquid equilibrium ratio used stage by stage in column design.
α₁₂ is the relative volatility; the further it is from 1, the easier the distillation.

sections.h3: Working backwards: γ from data and from an azeotrope

blocks.text: Measured P, x and y give activity coefficients directly, with no model: γ<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub> P/(x<sub>i</sub> P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>). Do this at every data point and you have the experimental γ(x) curve; fit a model through it.

An azeotrope is faster still. There x<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>, the composition cancels, and each component gives P = γ<sub>i</sub> P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>, so γ₁P₁<sup>sat</sup> = γ₂P₂<sup>sat</sup> = P. One azeotrope point therefore fixes two activity coefficients. Two γ values are enough to fix a two-parameter model: van Laar or two-parameter Margules is solved for both constants from γ₁ and γ₂ at the azeotropic composition. A one-parameter model such as Margules, ln γ₁ = A x₂² and ln γ₂ = A x₁², is over-determined: each γ gives its own A, and the two agree only if the model suits the system.

A minimum-boiling azeotrope has P above the ideal value, so γ<sub>i</sub> > 1 (positive deviation: unlike molecules attract each other less than like ones). A maximum-boiling azeotrope has P below it, so γ<sub>i</sub> < 1 (negative deviation: unlike molecules attract more).

The worked system below has one. At an azeotrope γ₁P₁<sup>sat</sup> = γ₂P₂<sup>sat</sup>, so ln(γ₁/γ₂) = A(x₂² − x₁²) = A(1 − 2x₁) = ln(P₂<sup>sat</sup>/P₁<sup>sat</sup>) = ln(20/60) = −1.0986. With A = 1.20, 1 − 2x₁ = −0.9155 and x₁ = 0.958, where P = 60.13 kPa, just above P₁<sup>sat</sup> = 60.0 kPa: a weak minimum-boiling azeotrope close to pure component 1.

figure.caption: The worked system at 343 K: positive deviation lifts the bubble curve far above the dashed Raoult line, giving 51.51 kPa instead of 36.0 at x₁ = 0.40, and the curves touch at a weak azeotrope near x₁ = 0.958.

spec.aria: P-x-y diagram at 343 K: a dashed straight ideal line from 20 to 60 kilopascals, a bowed bubble curve well above it and a dew curve below that; a tie line at 51.51 kilopascals joins x1 = 0.40 to y1 = 0.718, and the curves meet at an azeotrope near x1 = 0.958 and 60.13 kilopascals.

examples.question: At 343 K a binary liquid has x₁ = 0.40. The saturation pressures at 343 K are P₁<sup>sat</sup> = 60.0 kPa and P₂<sup>sat</sup> = 20.0 kPa. The liquid follows the one-parameter Margules model, ln γ₁ = A x₂² and ln γ₂ = A x₁², with A = 1.20. (a) Find the bubble pressure P and the vapour mole fraction y₁. (b) Compare with ideal Raoult's law.
steps: Partial pressures: x₁γ₁P₁<sup>sat</sup> = 0.40 × 1.5403 × 60.0 = 36.97 kPa; x₂γ₂P₂<sup>sat</sup> = 0.60 × 1.2116 × 20.0 = 14.54 kPa.
Vapour composition: y₁ = 36.97/51.51 = 0.7177 and y₂ = 14.54/51.51 = 0.2823; the sum is 1.0000, as it must be.
examples.answer: P = 51.51 kPa with y₁ = 0.7177, against 36.0 kPa and y₁ = 0.6667 from ideal Raoult's law: both γ exceed 1, a positive deviation.
examples.check:
import math
x1, x2 = 0.40, 0.60
P1s, P2s, A = 60.0, 20.0, 1.20
g1 = math.exp(A * x2**2)
g2 = math.exp(A * x1**2)
p1 = x1 * g1 * P1s
p2 = x2 * g2 * P2s
P = p1 + p2
y1 = p1 / P
Pid = x1 * P1s + x2 * P2s
y1id = x1 * P1s / Pid
print(round(g1, 4))
print(round(g2, 4))
print(round(P, 2))
print(round(y1, 4))
print(round(Pid, 1))
print(round(y1id, 4))

examples.question: Benzene(1)–toluene(2) is close to ideal. Find the bubble temperature and the first-vapour composition of a liquid with x₁ = 0.50 at 101.325 kPa. Antoine constants (ln P in kPa, T in °C): benzene A = 13.7819, B = 2726.81, C = 217.572; toluene A = 13.9320, B = 3056.96, C = 217.625.
steps: Saturation temperatures at 101.325 kPa, from T = B/(A − ln P) − C with ln 101.325 = 4.6183: benzene 2726.81/9.1636 − 217.572 = 80.0 °C; toluene 3056.96/9.3137 − 217.625 = 110.6 °C.

First guess, the mole-fraction average: T = 0.5 × 80.0 + 0.5 × 110.6 = 95.3 °C. Then P₁<sup>sat</sup> = 158.62 kPa, P₂<sup>sat</sup> = 64.26 kPa and Σx<sub>i</sub>P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> = 79.31 + 32.13 = 111.44 kPa, too high, so T is too high.
Second guess T = 90.0 °C: P₁<sup>sat</sup> = 136.50, P₂<sup>sat</sup> = 54.31 kPa, sum = 95.40 kPa, too low.

Interpolate: T = 90.0 + 5.3 × (101.325 − 95.40)/(111.44 − 95.40) = 91.96 °C, which gives a sum of 101.10 kPa. One more step gives T = 92.03 °C with P₁<sup>sat</sup> = 144.67 kPa, P₂<sup>sat</sup> = 57.97 kPa and a sum of 101.32 kPa.
examples.answer: The bubble temperature is 92.0 °C (365.2 K), and the first vapour has y₁ = 0.714.

traps: Applying plain Raoult's law to a pair with a known azeotrope. Ideal Raoult's law cannot produce an azeotrope at all unless the two P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> are equal, so it will badly misfit ethanol–water.
Evaluating γ<sub>i</sub> at the wrong composition. In the one-parameter Margules model γ₁ uses x₂² and γ₂ uses x₁²; swapping the two squares is the commonest slip in the exam hall.
Reading a dew point as a bubble point. At a dew point the given composition is y; substituting it as x gives a liquid far richer in the heavy component and the wrong pressure.

quiz.q: State Raoult's law and name the three assumptions behind it.
quiz.a: y<sub>i</sub> P = x<sub>i</sub> P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>. The assumptions are: ideal-gas vapour, φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> = 1; standard state is pure liquid i at the system T and P with negligible Poynting correction, f<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup>,pure ≈ P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>; and ideal solution, γ<sub>i</sub> = 1.

quiz.q: Why does benzene–toluene follow Raoult's law closely while ethanol–water does not?
quiz.a: Benzene and toluene are similar in size and polarity, so unlike and like contacts match and γ<sub>i</sub> stays near 1. Ethanol and water hydrogen-bond unequally, so γ<sub>i</sub> departs far from 1 and a minimum-boiling azeotrope forms.

quiz.q: At 350 K, x₁ = 0.30, γ₁ = 1.80, P₁<sup>sat</sup> = 80.0 kPa, γ₂ = 1.05, P₂<sup>sat</sup> = 40.0 kPa. Find the bubble pressure and y₁.
A measured point gives y₁ = 0.60 at P = 101.3 kPa, with x₁ = 0.30 and P₁<sup>sat</sup> = 120.0 kPa. Find γ₁.
At 320 K a binary mixture has an azeotrope at x₁ = 0.35 and P = 55.0 kPa, with P₁<sup>sat</sup> = 110.0 kPa and P₂<sup>sat</sup> = 70.0 kPa. Find γ₁ and γ₂ there and classify the deviation.
quiz.a: At an azeotrope x<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>, so γ<sub>i</sub> = P/P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>: γ₁ = 55.0/110.0 = 0.500 and γ₂ = 55.0/70.0 = 0.786. Both are below 1: negative deviation, a maximum-boiling azeotrope.

beyond: Not for the exam. Plant simulators fit NRTL or UNIQUAC to measured data, and UNIFAC predicts γ from molecular groups where no data exist. Search 'NRTL binary parameters' or 'entrainer selection'.
